page_hint: Ch 10, section 'Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients', paragraph 1 (final sentence)
quoted_clause: The sync cost, not compute, often caps DP at small scale unless the interconnect is fast.
observed: The sentence asserts that gradient-sync cost limits DP to *small* scale. The chapter's own ring model shows the opposite relationship: per-rank send volume is 2(N-1)/N x S, which is monotonically increasing but asymptotically flat in N. Sync time therefore does not grow materially with replica count; it is a fixed per-step tax. The binding fact is that the tax is large in absolute terms relative to a ~1 s step, at *any* N.
evidence: Recomputation from the section's own formula: per-rank send = 2(N-1)/N x 280 GB. N=2 -> 280 GB; N=8 -> 490 GB; N=16 -> 525 GB; N=64 -> 547 GB. At 25 GB/s: N=2 -> 11.2 s, N=8 -> 19.6 s, N=64 -> 21.9 s. At 450 GB/s: N=2 -> 0.62 s, N=8 -> 1.09 s, N=64 -> 1.22 s. So the sync cost is essentially N-independent; it does not 'cap DP at small scale', it caps DP *entirely* unless the interconnect is fast. The section's own numbers (19.6 s vs a ~1 s step at 25 GB/s; 1.09 s vs a ~1 s step even at 450 GB/s) support the 'absolute tax' reading, not the 'scale' reading.
root_cause: The ring normalization was applied to the byte count but not carried through to the scaling conclusion; 'scale' was used as a synonym for 'absolute overhead'.
correction: Replace with something like: 'Because ring all-reduce moves 2(N-1)/N x S per rank, the sync time is nearly independent of the replica count: adding DP replicas buys throughput at a fixed per-step tax rather than reducing the tax. DP is viable only when the interconnect is fast enough that this tax is a small fraction of the step (here 1.09 s at 450 GB/s against a ~1 s step - still marginal).'
acceptance_test: A reader who has read the section can state, without consulting the text, whether adding DP replicas increases or decreases per-step synchronization time, and can cite 2(N-1)/N as the reason. The phrase 'caps DP at small scale' no longer appears anywhere in the chapter.

page_hint: Ch 10, section 'Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients', paragraph 1 (the sentence 'this remains a communication model, not proof of training-state fit')

The decisive number for the canonical 70B model is missing, and the hedge is left as an unfulfilled promissory note. evidence: Independent rederivation for the canonical 70B model (70e9 params): BF16 weights 70e9 x 2 B = 140 GB; FP32 gradients 70e9 x 4 B = 280 GB; FP32 master weights = 280 GB; Adam m = 280 GB; Adam v = 280 GB. Total = 1,260 GB (~1.12 TB without master weights). Over 8 GPUs that is ~158 GB/GPU, still above the 80 GB HBM of an H100. So even FSDP across a full 8-GPU node does not hold Adam state in HBM; ZeRO-Offload / CPU Adam or >=16 shards is required. The training-state footprint is ~9x the weight footprint the section uses to justify its headline claim.

correction: Add a short paragraph giving the training-state budget (weights + gradients + optimizer states) for the canonical model and the resulting shard count, then tie it directly to the FSDP paragraph that follows. This also lets the section retire its own hedge with a number instead of a caveat.
acceptance_test: The section states a training-state byte total for the canonical 70B model and the resulting per-GPU requirement, and a reader can reconcile that figure with the FSDP discussion in the following paragraph.

page_hint: Ch 10, section '8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case', paragraph 2
quoted_clause: they verify the DP gradient-sync (if fine-tuning) stays under ~20% [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] of step time
observed: The chapter's own ring model makes this check unsatisfiable for the mini-case's 400B model. At the H100 NVLink directional peak of 450 GB/s: 3,200/450 = 7.1 s per step. At 25 GB/s: 3,200/25 = 128 s per step. A 20% budget therefore requires a step time of >= 35.6 s (NVLink) or >= 640 s (25 GB/s). The mini-case's own TPOT figures (80 ms -> 38 ms) imply a step time on the order of tens of milliseconds.

acceptance_test: A reader can compute the gradient-sync time for the mini-case's model from the chapter's own formulas and can state what configuration would bring it under 20% of step time.

page_hint: Ch 12 §7 (What We Still Don't Know), third bullet
quoted_clause: **P/D-disaggregation communication overhead in multi-host settings.** The KV-transfer volume and latency between prefill and decode pools — as a function of context length, request rate, and fabric bandwidth — is relatively unexplored at the 70B scale; the actual communication volume and its latency impact depend on the routing library and network topology **[HYPOTHESIS]**.

Leaving it as 'relatively unexplored' withholds the single most decision-relevant number for candidate (b), and it is the number that determines whether the two-pool design is even fabric-feasible at the canonical peak.
evidence: Independent re-derivation from the canonical inputs: each request transfers its KV once from the prefill pool to the decode pool. KV per request at the 9.5K context = 24.9 GB. At 10 rps average: 24.9 x 10 = 249 GB/s. At 40 rps peak: 24.9 x 40 = 996 GB/s (~1 TB/s) of sustained KV traffic, one-directional. Against fabric: a single 400 Gb/s InfiniBand NDR port is 50 GB/s, so the peak needs ~20 NDR ports or ~10 XDR (800 Gb/s) ports; a single H100 NVLink 4.0 link is 450 GB/s per direction, so ~3 links sustained at peak. The chapter's own §3 already flags the KV-transfer fabric as a cost item for candidate (b) ('plus the KV-transfer fabric'), so the number belongs in the chapter.
root_cause: The open-questions list was populated from what the author had not measured, without first checking which of the listed unknowns are already determined by the canonical inputs the chapter has adopted.

It does **not** mean one host serves the whole arrival rate; a single host is latency-bound and the peak capacity is a fleet-computing question (Ch17).
observed: The chapter's own headline says the canonical workload's deployment is a cluster, and its conclusion says the server tier is the right archetype. The distinction ('model-residency archetype' vs 'deployment tier') is real and carefully worded, but the reader is left without a single answer to the chapter's central question — 'which tier is the canonical workload in?' — and the two answers appear in the same section.
evidence: §3 opening: 'at the 40 rps peak its deployment is a **cluster** of ~21 server-class hosts'. §3 closing: 'the **server** tier is the right *model-residency* archetype'. The chapter title and the ladder in Fig 13.1 are framed around placement, so the reader expects one placement.
root_cause: The chapter needed to distinguish 'the tier whose memory budget the model fits' from 'the tier whose fleet the traffic requires', and the distinction was made by qualification rather than by naming two different questions.
correction: Name the two questions explicitly and answer both in one place: 'Two questions, two answers: the canonical workload's *residency* is server-class (the model and its KV fit one 8xH100 node), and its *deployment* is cluster-class (the 40 rps peak requires ~21-32 hosts). The ladder rung is chosen by the deployment question; the server tier is the unit of replication.' Then make the same two-question distinction in the chapter's opening and in Fig 13.1's caption.
acceptance_test: The chapter states one placement answer for the canonical workload, with the residency/deployment distinction made once and reused consistently.

evidence: Cross-chapter comparison: Ch 12 Table 12-1 (a) SLO cell = '? TTFT SLO unmeasured (Ch 14)'; Ch 13 §3 = 'Ch11's serving analysis indicates that ... keeps p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO'. Both are about a single 8xH100 host below capacity.

correction: Harmonize the wording: 'Ch 11's analytical serving model indicates that continuous batching + prefix caching should keep p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO on a single 8xH100 host below capacity; this remains an analytical indication until the Ch 14 measurement closes the SLO gate.'
